headline: German Budget Passes With €210 Billion in New Borrowing Planned
author: Kamil Kowalcze

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Germany's parliament approved a €556 billion ($610 billion) budget that will ramp up spending on defense and infrastructure by piling on more debt.

The finance plan for 2027 that Chancellor Friedrich Merz succeeded in passing through the Bundestag on Friday is almost 6% larger than the one for this year, and is set to require more than €210 billion in net new borrowing.

More than half of core expenditure is earmarked either for labor and social affairs or for defense, highlighting both the increasing strain caused by Germany's welfare state and the government's focus on a rapid buildup in the military.

The legislative milestone reached in Berlin follows a hard-fought deal between Merz's conservative bloc and the Social Democrats of Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil that followed months of coalition disputes over taxes, welfare spending and borrowing.
"The process of drawing up this budget certainly did not deserve a beauty prize," the chancellor told lawmakers earlier this week.
Talks continued into the final days, with the parties agreeing to lower an electricity tax for households and businesses, and to soften previously agreed welfare cuts.
The coalition is also using debt-financed special funds to modernize the military and infrastructure after decades of under-investment.

Merz warned that this round of bargaining was only the beginning, saying that Germany will no longer be able to finance everything citizens have come to expect from tax revenue. The government's financial plan still contains an unresolved shortfall of more than €20 billion for 2028.

Of the planned net new borrowing, about €123 billion is assigned to the core budget. A further €58 billion will come through the infrastructure and climate-neutrality fund, with roughly €30 billion allocated to the Bundeswehr special fund.

Much of the borrowing falls outside the normal limits of Germany's constitutional debt brake, allowing Klingbeil to increase spending on rearmament and infrastructure while seeking savings elsewhere in the regular budget.
Labor and social affairs remains the largest ministry budget at €203 billion. Defense receives about €110 billion from the core budget and almost €30 billion more from the military special fund.
Debt-servicing costs will rise by more than a third to about €41 billion.
The legislation will now go to the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house, which is due to meet on Dec. 18.
